South Korea accuses North Korea of firing ballistic missile towards its east coast

Just last month, South Korea had blamed North Korea for a landmine blast in the Demilitarized Zone that injured three South Korean soldiers.

Myungshin Cho

03 October, 2026 12:35 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

A North Korean flag flutters at the propaganda village of Gijungdong in North Korea, in this picture taken near the truce village of Panmunjom inside the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating the two Koreas, South Korea, July 19, 2022. REUTERS/Kim Hong-Ji/Pool

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

North Korea fired a ballistic missile toward its east coast on Saturday, South Korea’s defense ministry said, adding tension to already fraught ties between the neighbors over landmine blasts near the border last month.

The missile was launched from the Wonsan area on North Korea’s east coast at around 6:30 a.m. local time and traveled more than 700 kilometers (435 miles), South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement. Seoul’s military said it has strengthened surveillance and readiness and is analyzing the projectile’s specifications with US authorities.

South Korea’s National Security Office convened an emergency security meeting to assess the impact of the North Korean test on security and to take necessary measures. The Seoul government urged the North to immediately halt the launches, which it said violate UN Security Council resolutions.

Show Full Article

The latest missile test is North Korea’s second in the last month and comes amid accusations by Seoul that Pyongyang was responsible for a landmine blast in the Demilitarized Zone that injured three South Korean soldiers. The North’s launches underscore leader Kim Jong Un’s confidence that he can pursue weapons development unhindered, and highlight the threat it poses in the region.

South Korea has demanded an apology from the North over the mine blast, with the UN Command describing it as a violation of the armistice between the two nations. Pyongyang has denied involvement and derided the probe into the explosion as a “farce.”

Kim has been deepening strategic ties with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and continues close coordination with China in a growing alignment among the three nations against a US-led security order, even as President Donald Trump has made fresh overtures to revive a dialogue with Pyongyang.

The North Korean leader’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has also warned that the country will consider new military strategies in response to Japan’s expanding defense capabilities, saying Pyongyang would not remain a “passive onlooker.”

In its latest annual threat assessment report, the US intelligence authorities said North Korea had “successfully tested” intercontinental ballistic missiles capable of reaching the entire US mainland and gained “valuable war-fighting experience and military technology from Russia for participating in combat operations against Ukraine.”

Japan has said in its latest defense white paper that North Korea has been demonstrating “extremely rapid” progress in missile development, including advanced hypersonic missiles, following Kim’s military pact with Putin agreed to in 2024.

–With assistance from Soo-Hyang Choi.

PoV

Yamal and Mbappé don’t deserve the Ballon d’Or

Lamine Yamal has a World Cup. Kylian Mbappé has 58 goals. Neither has done enough to bag the Ballon d’Or.

Mohammad Hammad

03 October, 2026 10:52 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Kylian Mbappe (L) and Lamine Yamal are the favourites of this year to win the Ballon d'Or | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

F or almost 15 years, Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo made the Ballon d’Or—football’s most prestigious individual award—their own private battleground. The duo dominated the game, scored goals, broke records and won almost every major title there was. Most importantly, they did their talking on the pitch .

This year, the battle feels different.

After the fierce competition between two all-time greats, we now have a “beg-to-beg” competition between French striker Kylian Mbappe and Spanish winger Lamine Yamal. B oth are self-advocating their brilliance in the media, claiming they have done enough to win the award.

Show Full Article

Their individual brilliance is undeniable, and the numbers speak for themselves. But when those individual achievements are measured against their teams’ actual success, the tall claims become a little harder to swallow.

Have they actually done enough to deserve the Ballon d’Or?

Weak case for Yamal and Mbappe Yamal’s Ballon d’Or claim is heavily built around Spain’s World Cup triumph, but his individual numbers at the tournament leave a lot to be desired. He finished the World Cup with just one goal and one assist. Of course, context matters. Yamal entered the tournament after recovering from an injury and following an exhausting season with Barcelona, where he was a key figure in their domestic success, scoring 16 goals and providing 12 assists.

While he was the player of the season in La Liga, Barcelona’s biggest ambition — winning the Champions League — remained an unfulfilled dream since 2015. They were knocked out in the quarter-finals by Diego Simeone’s Atlético Madrid. So, when we look at Yamal’s entire season rather than just the World Cup and Spain’s success, does his resume truly make him the standout player of the year? No, it doesn’t.

Then there is Mbappé, whose case is almost entirely built around his numbers. And this is where the debate becomes particularly interesting.

Mbappé finished as the top scorer across all major competitions with 58 goals for club and country: 25 in La Liga, 15 in the Champions League and 10 for France at the World Cup.

On paper, those numbers are extraordinary. But let’s put these numbers into perspective.

Mbappé scored 25 goals in La Liga, but only 17 came from open play — fewer than Vedat Muriqi of Mallorca, whose side was relegated last season. In the Champions League, Mbappé won the Golden Boot with 15 goals, but 13 of those came during the initial league phase, against opponents such as Benfica, Marseille, Kairat, Monaco and Olympiacos.

His World Cup campaign, however, is much harder to question. He won the Golden Boot after scoring 10 goals. But even that achievement came with a caveat: his final goal tally was boosted by his hat-trick in the third-place play-off against England, a match English forward Harry Kane did not play.

And then there is the bigger picture: Mbappé ended another season without a major trophy.

That makes his own claim particularly fascinating. Mbappé has said: “For years, I’ve considered myself the best player in the world. I haven’t seen anyone better than me.” He also said he would accept Messi or Ronaldo winning the Ballon d’Or, but he would not have swapped places with anyone else who has won it.

But would the recent winners have wanted to swap places with him?

Would Luka Modrić, who led Croatia to a historic World Cup F inal in 2018 , have traded his Ballon d’Or for Mbappé’s goals? Would Karim Benzema, Rodri or Ousmane Dembélé? Would they have exchanged their trophies, titles and defining moments for individual numbers?

That, for me, is where the Ballon d’Or debate becomes more complicated.

Also read: Cristiano Ronaldo’s Portugal exit is another selfish tantrum. He is ruining his legacy

Goals alone won’t suffice Individual numbers matter, goals matter. But football is ultimately a team sport, and individual brilliance becomes far more significant when it is backed by collective success — unless the numbers are so extraordinary that they become impossible to ignore, like Messi’s 91 goals in 2012.

This isn’t an argument against Mbappé. His numbers are remarkable, and his World Cup campaign was exceptional. But after almost a decade at the very top of football, his defining achievement remains the 2018 World Cup.

Let’s remember Mbappe plays for two of the biggest teams in Real Madrid and France, where numbers should also translate into the team’s achievements.

Because if goals alone are supposed to be the strongest argument for the Ballon d’Or, then why isn’t Harry Kane making the same case?

Kane has scored 73 goals across all competitions this season — 15 more than Mbappe.

Meanwhile, m any are backing Messi to win it for the record ninth time after a magical World Cup run from the little maestro at the age of 39. Messi scored eight goals and provided four assists—two of which came against England in the semi-finals. At 39, Messi once again showed why he’s still in contention for the golden ball.

Although the award is slowly losing its credibility, and with this being the World Cup year, the winner will surely be scrutinised. The debate and claims are only going to catch fire as there are no clear favourites this time. But the self-advocacy outburst of Mbappe and Yamal is surely a bit too far from what they managed to achieve. While Yamal’s Spain and Barcelona bested Mbappe’s France and Real Madrid, this doesn’t mean that he was the point of difference every time the two met on the field.

While Harry Kane also failed to secure anything big with his team and Messi is not playing in Europe, it’ll be interesting to see who takes home the award on 26 October.

(Edited by Saptak Datta)

Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war is hitting India’s food and fertiliser security. Delhi has a role to play

The Black Sea region accounts for roughly a third of global wheat trade and 63% of the world’s sunflower oil exports. Food could be the next crisis for emerging economies.

Parthiva Bhaumik

03 October, 2026 09:18 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Smoke rises from a civilian vessel on fire in the Black Sea off Odesa, Ukraine, on 19 July 2026 | Photo credit: Reuters/Stringer

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

F or much of the developing world, the defining shortage of the next two years may not be energy or credit. It may be food. Wheat prices are at a two-year high, fertiliser costs are climbing, and the shipping routes that carry staple grain to import-dependent countries are becoming harder to insure and use. Much of this traces to one stretch of water.

The Black Sea region accounts for roughly a third of global wheat trade and 63 per cent of the world’s sunflower oil exports . Its ports in Ukraine supply food products to more than 55 countries . India is among them, and among the most exposed. It is the world’s largest buyer of sunflower oil, and sources most of it from the Black Sea. It also depends on the same waters for important fertiliser supply lines.

India has spent the last few years arguing that the food and fertiliser security of developing countries cannot be left at the mercy of distant conflicts. It pressed the case through its G20 presidency and the Voice of the Global South summits and has been among the few large economies willing to speak for countries that import what they eat but control none of the routes their food travels on. For countries that buy their food in dollars and subsidise staples at home, a disruption thousands of miles away can very quickly become a problem for government budgets and household kitchens.

Show Full Article

The danger is no longer abstract for Indians either. In July, the Golden Leo , a cargo ship sailing from Ukraine, was struck by Russian cruise missiles off the Greater Odesa port. Nine of its seventeen crew members were killed, including four Indians . India already supplies more than 12 per cent of the global maritime workforce. With the government aiming for one in five seafarers worldwide to be Indian, attacks on commercial shipping put Indian maritime professionals disproportionately at risk.

This could hardly come at a worse time for India. Exporters are already being squeezed by US tariffs, while sanctions risk over Russian oil purchases and disruption at major energy chokepoints are pushing up costs across the economy. Food and fertiliser now threaten to become a third shock, arriving just as India is trying to absorb the first two.

Also Read: How Ukrainian assault on Russia’s largest Black Sea terminal threatens India’s crude imports

Food and fertiliser shocks hit India In India, the effects are already visible in cooking oil. Sunflower oil shipments from the Black Sea have been delayed by up to 60 days, and India’s imports have fallen 24 per cent this season to 2.48 million tonnes. Meanwhile, soybean oil purchases have risen 54 per cent as refiners look for alternatives.

Crude sunflower oil landed in India at around $1,496 a tonne in August, 18.4 per cent above the previous year. By comparison, palm oil prices rose 9.4 per cent and soybean oil 7.9 per cent.

Delhi has already cut import duties on edible oils, with the deepest reduction on sunflower oil, giving up revenue to limit the effect on consumers. Refiners are increasingly looking to Argentina , which has overtaken Ukraine as a supplier to India for the first time. But finding oil elsewhere is proving more expensive. Longer journeys add to costs just as more countries are competing for the same suppliers.

The second channel is fertiliser, and here the fiscal exposure is even larger. India relies heavily on imports from the Black Sea region and the Gulf, leaving it exposed to upheavals in both conflict zones. To avoid disruption in the Gulf, India has already rerouted procurement to Egypt, Algeria, Nigeria and Georgia. The Union Budget for 2026-27 allocated Rs 1.71 lakh crore for fertiliser subsidies, but the government may now need an additional Rs 70,000-80,000 crore as higher import costs push the bill well beyond budget. Subsidy spending on imported urea alone rose 128 per cent last year to nearly Rs 48,000 crore. A budget written on the assumption of easing global prices is being overtaken by the opposite.

Also Read: Ukraine’s robotic army is already at work. India must rethink the next battlefield

Delhi has leverage others don’t The wider problem is one India has spent the past decade warning about: countries across the Global South are forced to absorb shocks they did little to create. Bangladeshi buyers are now paying more than $450 a tonne for Australian wheat that cost under $380 before the disruption; replacing Black Sea supply can add another $25-60 a tonne. Somalia imports 90 per cent of its cereals, with six million people already facing acute hunger. These are the countries India has increasingly sought to speak for, and this time it is feeling the same pressure itself.

There is another reason for Delhi to become involved. India has consistently presented itself as a country willing to engage both sides in pursuit of peace, even when that position has attracted criticism.

An arrangement focused on protecting commercial food shipments would address an immediate problem shared by countries far beyond Europe while giving practical weight to its commitment to peace. It could start modestly with a food corridor between Indian and Black Sea ports, using Indian-flagged ships carrying grain, edible oil and fertiliser already bought by Indian buyers, with Indian maritime observers on board rather than military escorts. Striking an identifiable Indian ship carrying food to India or the Global South would carry a very different cost.

India also has leverage few others do. Its substantial economic relationship with Moscow gives Delhi a degree of access and economic weight that many countries simply do not have. It can use that position to press Moscow not to target civilian ships or the ports serving them, and to make the protection of commercial shipping part of the wider economic conversation between the two countries.

For India, this is no longer a distant war with distant consequences. Its seafarers are at risk, its food and fertiliser costs are rising, and the countries it has promised to speak for are being hit even harder. The Black Sea gives Delhi a rare chance to protect its own interests, stand up for the Global South and show what its commitment to peace can deliver in practice.

Parthiva Bhaumik is an analyst with the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change based in Kyiv. Views are personal.

Man accused of ex-minister murder charged with preparing terrorist acts against Reform UK’s Nigel Farage

Reuters

03 October, 2026 01:30 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Michael Holden LONDON, Oct 2 (Reuters) – British police said on Friday that a man accused of murdering former minister Ann Widdecombe had now also been charged with preparing acts of terrorism, including against Nigel Farage, the leader of the populist Reform UK party.

Police and prosecutors said Joshua Kerry, 28, had been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation of terrorist acts between May 2024 and July this year, saying that these related in part to Farage.

They did not provide further details. Kerry, from Rotherham in northern England, is due to appear at London’s Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday.

Show Full Article

“We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time,” Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said in a statement.

“The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the counter terrorism policing network.”

FORMER MINISTER ‘MURDERED AT HOME’

Kerry is already facing accusations of murdering Widdecombe, 78, a prominent figure in Reform UK, who was found dead at her home in rural southwest England on July 9 after being attacked the day before.

The killing of Widdecombe, who prosecutors said was struck 21 times with a hammer, shocked British politics, raising further concerns about politicians’ security, with two serving British members of parliament having been killed since 2016.

“Terrifying. Widdecombe alleged murderer charged with acts of terrorism against Nigel Farage over 2 years,” Reform lawmaker Richard Tice wrote on X. “This is why he needs money for security.”

Farage, 62, often credited with forcing the 2016 referendum on whether Britain should stay in the European Union, has been one of the most influential, but also one of the most divisive, figures in British politics for more than a decade.

When campaigning for parliament in 2024, Farage had a milkshake thrown at him by a woman and on another occasion objects were hurled towards his open-top bus by a man.

Reform UK was leading in the polls until recently, though a combination of allegations over party funding and Andy Burnham taking over as prime minister has seen an erosion in its support.

Farage is currently facing a parliamentary investigation over whether he should have declared a £5 million ($6.75 million) gift from a billionaire cryptocurrency investor. He has since said the money was necessary to provide him with security.

“This is exactly why Nigel needed £5m to protect his security for life,” a Reform UK source told Reuters.

British Home Secretary (interior minister) Shabana Mahmood said the latest charges were extremely concerning.

“My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family,” she said on X. “Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all. This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life.”

(Additional reporting by Sam Tobin and Elizabeth Piper; Editing by Cynthia Osterman and Alistair Bell)
